processing: Large-leaf cultivars are made as full black tea: withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried, as is standard for the class.
harvest_season: Specific picking calendars are not well recorded in plain terms; ask the seller for the season and the cultivar.
appearance_dry: Long, dark twisted leaf, as is typical of large-leaf black tea.
appearance_liquor: Clear reddish amber, typical of large-leaf black tea.
appearance_wet: Broad coppery brown leaves, as you would expect from an Assam-type plant.
taste_profile: As with other black teas from Assam-type large-leaf plants, expect a full, malty body and real briskness. The character shifts with the cultivar, so an Assam lot and a No. 18 lot will not taste the same.

brewing.notes: Large-leaf black tea can turn tannic, so start with short steeps and water a little below boiling. For a mug, use 3 g in 250 ml for about three minutes.

vintage_note: Usual for Taiwanese black tea: sold by harvest year and often by cultivar, and at its best fresh, within a year or two. A label naming the cultivar, such as No. 18 or Assam, tells you more than the lake's name alone. A government certification mark also exists for this tea, so look for it on the pack.
description:
Sun Moon Lake black tea comes from the hills around Taiwan's best-known lake, in Yuchi township in Nantou. It is counted among Taiwan's ten famous teas, and it stands out on an island better known for oolong: a big-leaf black tea built on Assam stock.

The name covers several cultivars. Assam and TTES No. 7 and No. 8 are grown here, but the tea people ask for by name is TTES No. 18, called Hongyu or Red Jade, bred locally at the Yuchi branch of the tea research station. Gardens sit at about 500 to 800 metres, where the area's steady humidity and temperatures suit big-leaf plants.

Red Jade is the one with the signature smell, usually described as cinnamon and mint. Like other large-leaf black teas it has plenty of body and can bite if overbrewed, so keep the steeps short and adjust from there.

When buying, ask which cultivar you are getting, since the name alone does not tell you. A certified mark or a named Yuchi producer is more useful than the lake on the label.
history:
Large-leaf tea from Assam was brought in during the Japanese era by the technician Arai Kokichiro, and Yuchi became the centre of black tea making for this type. The name itself is much later: Nantou county magistrate Liu Yu-you named it Sun Moon Lake black tea in 1978.

The Yuchi branch of the Tea Research and Extension Station went on to promote TTES No. 18 as the area's top black tea, and a local industry association markets a hand-picked Assam line.
